section.title: The Great Banquet and the Cost of Discipleship
section.sectionRationale: At a Sabbath meal in a Pharisee's house, Jesus heals a man with dropsy, then overturns the table manners of the proud: take the lowest place, and invite those who cannot repay you. When a guest speaks of the blessedness of the kingdom's feast, Jesus tells of a great banquet whose invited guests all make excuses, so the master fills his house with the poor from the streets and the highways. Then, to the crowds who follow so easily, He names the cost: whoever will not carry his cross and give up everything cannot be His disciple.
section.thesis: The kingdom is a banquet of free grace that gathers the poor and the outsider while the self-satisfied excuse themselves, and it lays a total claim on all who would follow, so that grace which costs the sinner nothing costs the disciple everything.
section.frameNote: Four movements: healing on the Sabbath and the places at the table; the invitation of those who cannot repay; the parable of the great banquet; and the cost of discipleship, with the warning of savorless salt.

units.label: The Sabbath meal and the places of honor
units.note: the one who humbles himself will be exalted

verses.text: One Sabbath, Jesus went to eat in the home of a leading Pharisee, and those in attendance were watching Him closely.
Right there before Him was a man with dropsy.
So Jesus asked the experts in the law and the Pharisees, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath or not?”
But they remained silent. Then Jesus took hold of the man, healed him, and sent him on his way.
And He asked them, “Which of you whose son or ox falls into a pit on the Sabbath day will not immediately pull him out?”
And they were unable to answer these questions.
When Jesus noticed how the guests chose the places of honor, He told them a parable:
“When you are invited to a wedding banquet, do not sit in the place of honor, in case someone more distinguished than you has been invited.
Then the host who invited both of you will come and tell you, ‘Give this man your seat.’ And in humiliation, you will have to take the last place.

But when you are invited, go and sit in the last place, so that your host will come and tell you, ‘Friend, move up to a better place.’ Then you will be honored in front of everyone at the table with you.
For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who {{tapeinoo|humbles}} himself will be exalted.”

units.label: Inviting those who cannot repay
units.note: you will be repaid at the resurrection

verses.text: Then Jesus said to the man who had invited Him, “When you host a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or brothers or relatives or rich neighbors. Otherwise, they may invite you in return, and you will be repaid.
But when you host a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind,
and you will be blessed. Since they cannot repay you, you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.”

units.label: The parable of the great banquet

verses.text: When one of those reclining with Him heard this, he said to Jesus, “Blessed is everyone who will eat at the feast in the kingdom of God.”
But Jesus replied, “A certain man prepared a great banquet and invited many guests.
When it was time for the banquet, he sent his servant to tell those who had been invited, ‘Come, for everything is now ready.’
But one after another they all began to make excuses. The first one said, ‘I have bought a field, and I need to go see it. Please excuse me.’
Another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to try them out. Please excuse me.’
Still another said, ‘I have married a wife, so I cannot come.’

The servant returned and reported all this to his master. Then the owner of the house became angry and said to his servant, ‘Go out quickly into the streets and alleys of the city, and bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame.’
‘Sir,’ the servant replied, ‘what you ordered has been done, and there is still room.’
So the master told his servant, ‘Go out to the highways and hedges and {{anankazo|compel}} them to come in, so that my house will be full.
For I tell you, not one of those men who were invited will taste my banquet.’”

units.label: The cost of discipleship and savorless salt
units.note: whoever does not carry his cross

verses.text: Now large crowds were traveling with Jesus, and He turned and said to them,
“If anyone comes to Me and does not {{miseo|hate}} his father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, even his own life, he cannot be My disciple.
And whoever does not carry his {{stauros|cross}} and follow Me cannot be My disciple.
Which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost to see if he has the resources to complete it?
Otherwise, if he lays the foundation and is unable to finish the work, everyone who sees it will ridicule him,
saying, ‘This man could not finish what he started to build.’
Or what king on his way to war with another king will not first sit down and consider whether he can engage with ten thousand men the one coming against him with twenty thousand?
And if he is unable, he will send a delegation while the other king is still far off, to ask for terms of peace.
In the same way, any one of you who does not give up everything he has cannot be My disciple.
Salt is good, but if the salt loses its savor, with what will it be seasoned?
It is fit neither for the soil nor for the manure pile, and it is thrown out. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

tapeinoo.gloss: To humble, to lower. Jesus lays down the law of the kingdom against the scramble for status at the table: everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who lowers himself will be lifted up by God. This is the pattern of Christ Himself, who humbled Himself and was exalted.

anankazo.gloss: To compel, to constrain, to urge strongly. The master sends his servant to the highways and hedges to compel the outsiders in, not by force of violence but by the pressing, gracious urgency of the invitation, so that his house will be full. The word underlines that grace goes out and draws the reluctant and the unlikely.

miseo.gloss: To hate. In Semitic idiom to hate is to love less, to subordinate. Jesus is not commanding hostility to family but demanding that loyalty to Him surpass every other bond, even the love of one's own life. Christ must be first, or He is not truly followed at all.

stauros.gloss: Cross. To carry one's cross is to walk as a condemned man walks to execution, dead to the old self and its claims. Jesus makes cross-bearing the mark of a true disciple, a daily death that anticipates His own and shares in it.

basic.context: At a Pharisee's Sabbath table, Jesus heals a man with dropsy and silences those who watched to trap Him. Seeing guests grab the best seats, He teaches them to take the lowest place, for God exalts the humble. He tells the host to invite those who cannot repay, the poor and the lame, promising repayment at the resurrection. When a guest sighs about the blessedness of the kingdom's feast, Jesus tells of a great banquet: the invited guests all make excuses, so the master fills his house with the poor from the streets and strangers from the highways. Then, to the crowds who follow so lightly, He names the cost: whoever will not put Him above family and self, carry his cross, and give up everything cannot be His disciple. Salt that loses its savor is thrown out.
basic.hermeneutics: Hold the two halves together. The banquet parables proclaim grace: the feast is free, and it fills up with those who could never earn a place. The discipleship sayings name the cost: this free grace lays total claim on the one who receives it. Grace that costs the sinner nothing costs the disciple everything.
basic.originalLanguages: The law of the table is that the one who tapeinoo, humbles himself, will be exalted. The master sends out to anankazo, to compel, the outsiders in by gracious urgency. To follow Jesus one must miseo, love less, every rival loyalty, even life itself, and carry the stauros, the cross, the daily death of a condemned man.
basic.typology: The kingdom feast fulfills the prophets' picture of a great banquet God spreads for all peoples on His mountain. The rejected invitation and the gathering of outsiders foreshadow the gospel going out from Israel to the nations. Cross-bearing points to Christ's own cross, the pattern every disciple takes up.
basic.christ: Jesus is the Lord of the Sabbath who heals and the host of the kingdom banquet who throws His house open to the poor. He is the One who humbled Himself and was exalted, the pattern of the table's law. And He is the King worth more than father, mother, and life itself, who calls His followers to the cross He will Himself carry.
basic.god: God exalts the humble and welcomes those who cannot repay, delighting to fill His house with the overlooked. He is generous beyond calculation, promising repayment at the resurrection. And He is worthy of total allegiance, a Father whose feast is free yet whose claim is absolute.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 25 pictures the LORD's feast of rich food for all peoples. Philippians 2 shows Christ humbled and then exalted. Luke 9 gives the parallel call to take up the cross daily. James 4 promises that God lifts up the humble.
basic.oneStory: On the road to Jerusalem Jesus spreads the kingdom's table wide, gathering the poor and the outsider while the comfortable excuse themselves. The same grace that fills His house for free lays a cross on every guest, so that the story runs from the open invitation of the banquet to the total surrender of the disciple who follows the humbled and exalted King.

context.literary:
Luke 14 is built around a single Sabbath meal and then walks out of the house onto the road. It has the shape of a table conversation that keeps widening: the first scene is a question put to experts in the law, 14:1-6; the second addresses the guests, 14:7-11; the third addresses the host, 14:12-14; the fourth answers a guest's pious remark, 14:15-24; and the last turns to the crowds outside, 14:25-35. Each speech answers the one before it. The man who claims the highest seat is told to take the lowest, the host who invites the rich is told to invite the poor, and the guest who sighs about the kingdom's feast is told how easily invited people stay away.

Luke loves a meal as a place of revelation. Jesus eats with Levi's friends in Luke 5:29, with Simon the Pharisee in 7:36, and with another Pharisee in 11:37, and each time the table exposes who is really welcome. The verb that opens this scene, 'watching Him closely,' belongs to the same family of watchfulness Luke uses of hostile observers in 6:7 and 20:20. The host's guests are the ones under observation, though they do not know it.

The parable carries its own careful structure. A first summons goes out, 14:16-17; three excuses come back, 14:18-20; the master sends the servant out twice, first to the streets and alleys of the city, 14:21, then, with the house still not full, 14:22, to the highways and hedges beyond it, 14:23. The healing in 14:1-6 and the banquet in 14:15-24 are bookends: a sick man is welcomed to the table of a hostile host, and the poor are welcomed to the table of a rejected host.

The chapter then closes with three short illustrations, the tower, the king and the salt, 14:28-35. The first two begin with the same rhetorical question, 'Which of you,' the form Jesus used in 14:5 against the silent lawyers, so that the whole chapter is held together by questions that cannot be answered without self-examination.
context.historical:
A Sabbath meal in a prominent house was a public event. Guests reclined on couches at a table ordered by rank, and where you were placed announced where you stood in the village. The Greek word for the places of honor, 14:7, is the one Jesus uses again in Luke 20:46 of the scribes who love the best seats at feasts. The advice of 14:8-10 is not a trick for gaining honor; it is conventional wisdom already given in Proverbs 25:6-7, and the BSB footnote at 14:10 points to that text.

Hospitality worked as a ledger of favors. A host invited those who could invite him back, so that dinners circulated status among equals, and the language of 'repaid' in 14:12 and 14:14 is the vocabulary of that exchange. To invite the poor, the crippled, the lame and the blind was to step outside the whole economy. One text among the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Rule of the Congregation, keeps people with such disabilities out of the assembly of the end times, which shows how natural it was in some circles to imagine the messianic banquet as a gathering of the whole and the pure. Jesus' guest list is the reverse.

The man with dropsy, 14:2, was suffering from swelling caused by fluid, and Jesus' answer to the lawyers rests on the common practice of rescuing a beast from a pit on the Sabbath, 14:5. In the parable, the three excuses involve land, five yoke of oxen, which is a sizeable farming outfit, and a marriage. None is an emergency, and buying a field or a team without first seeing it is the kind of excuse nobody expects to be believed. When a great man gave a banquet, a second call was sent when the meal was ready, and to refuse at that point was a public insult to the host.

The call to count the cost of a tower or of a war, 14:28-32, drew on ordinary experience: a half-built tower left standing was a familiar sight, and a small king facing a larger army had to negotiate. The crowds, large and traveling with Him, 14:25, were on the road to Jerusalem, and the road is where the invitation became a decision.
context.canonical:
The image of a feast set by God runs through the whole Bible. Isaiah 25:6-8 describes a banquet on the mountain for all peoples where death itself is swallowed up, and Isaiah 55:1-2 calls the thirsty and the penniless to come and eat without money. The guest's exclamation in Luke 14:15 draws on that hope, and Jesus' reply says that the hope is being offered now and that many who expect a seat are refusing it. Matthew 22:1-14 tells a related parable of a wedding feast, with its own details, and Revelation 19:9 pronounces blessed those invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb, so the feast is also the destination of the story.

The law of the table, 14:11, is an old reversal. Hannah sang that the Lord brings low and exalts, 1 Samuel 2:7-8, and Mary echoes her in Luke 1:52, and Luke repeats the saying about exalting and humbling in 18:14. James 4:6 and 4:10 and 1 Peter 5:5-6 draw the same line for the church, and Proverbs 3:34, quoted in both, supplies the root: God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble.

The invitation to the poor and the excluded points back to the lists of Luke 4:18 and 7:22, where good news is preached to the poor and the lame walk, and forward to Acts, where the invitation goes out to Samaritans and Gentiles. The excuses of 14:18-20 sound like the three exemptions from battle in Deuteronomy 20:5-7, which were granted to a man with a new house, a vineyard or a betrothed wife. What was a mercy in war has become, in the parable, a way to avoid the feast.

The cost of following is spoken again and again in Luke: 9:23-26, 9:57-62 and 18:22. The saying about leaving family is echoed in Matthew 10:37. Hebrews 13:12-14 asks believers to go to Him outside the camp, bearing His reproach, which is the same cross-shaped road.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wants his readers, many of them gentile and many of them comfortable, to see that the kingdom is not a club that rewards the well placed. Every part of this chapter takes away a reason for confidence. The lawyers cannot defend their silence about healing, the guests cannot defend their grasping for rank, the host cannot defend his closed list, the invited cannot defend their excuses, and the crowd cannot defend an easy following.

The author also leaves the reader with a pair of tasks that belong together. First, receive: the feast is ready and the servant is still going out, so that the poor and the unlikely, who know they have no claim, are the ones who fill the house. Second, count: the same Jesus who gives the invitation says plainly that the road costs everything the follower owns. Luke does not resolve this by softening either half. He is writing for people who need to hear, in the same breath, that they are wanted and that they must not drift.

Two details show the care of the writing. The servant says in 14:22 that there is 'still room,' which is an open door for the reader, and the master's final judgment in 14:24 is spoken to the guests of the story, not to the invited reader who is still deciding. The invitation is therefore live as Luke tells it. And the chapter ends with 'He who has ears to hear, let him hear,' a line that hands the whole matter back to the hearer.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The healing is a record of something Jesus did; the sayings about seats, guest lists and cost are given as instructions. The distinction matters because the rank of seats is not a rule for banquet etiquette but a principle of how people treat honor, and the guest list of 14:13 is not a ban on dinner parties with friends. Jesus uses an overstatement to make a point about where generosity should aim, and the same style appears in the 'hating' of 14:26.

The parable of the banquet describes what happens to an invitation that is ignored. It is not a pattern to copy, since no disciple is the master of the house. What does carry over is the movement of the story: the servant goes out, the reluctant are urged, and the house fills. The church is the servant, and the work belongs to anyone who has been fed at the table.

The cost sayings are direct commands to anyone who would follow. They do not set a ladder for the elite among believers, since the crowds addressed in 14:25 are ordinary people. They are also not a program of self-punishment: the point of the tower and the king is to reckon honestly and then to go on, and the point of the salt is usefulness. What is prescriptive is the order of loyalties, with Christ first, and the readiness to let go of possessions, 14:33, when they stand in His way.

debates.question: What does Jesus mean by commanding disciples to 'hate' father and mother?

views.label: A Semitic idiom for loving less, radical priority
views.case: In Hebrew and Aramaic thought, to hate can mean to love less or to subordinate, as when Jacob is said to love Leah less. Matthew's parallel reads 'loves father or mother more than Me', confirming that Jesus demands supreme allegiance, not literal hostility. He elsewhere upholds honoring parents.

views.label: A deliberately shocking absolute
views.case: The starkness is intended: discipleship may set a follower against his own household, and Jesus refuses to soften the break that loyalty to Him can require. The word is chosen to jolt casual crowds into weighing the true cost.

debates.bearing: Either way the point stands: Christ must hold first place over every other love, including the love of one's own life, or discipleship is not real. This is priority, not permission for cruelty.

debates.question: What does 'compel them to come in' authorize?

views.label: The urgent, gracious persuasion of the gospel
views.case: The master's aim is a full house of the unlikely; the compelling is the pressing insistence of an invitation that overcomes the poor's reluctance to believe they are truly welcome. The context is grace overflowing to those who assume they do not belong.

views.label: A text tragically misused to justify coercion
views.case: In history this line was wrongly wielded to force conversions. Read rightly against the whole passage of free invitation and undeserving guests, it cannot mean violence; it means the earnest, winning urgency of a servant sent to gather the reluctant.

debates.bearing: The verse fuels bold, warm evangelism to those who feel unqualified, never coercion; the God of this banquet draws the outsider by grace, not by force.

debates.question: Who are the two groups of guests the servant gathers?

views.label: The outcasts of Israel, then the Gentiles
views.case: The first errand is to the streets and alleys of the city, 14:21, and the second to the highways and hedges, 14:23, outside it. Many read the first as the poor and sinners within Israel, whom Jesus was already gathering, and the second as the nations beyond, the movement traced in Acts. The master's verdict in 14:24 then speaks to the first invited, who forfeit their places.

views.label: One continuing mission to the needy
views.case: Others hold that the two errands are a single movement of ever-widening invitation and need not be mapped onto Jew and gentile. The point of the second errand is simply that there is still room, 14:22, and that the master will not stop until the house is full.

debates.bearing: Both readings keep the center: God's house fills with those who know they cannot repay, and the invitation does not close while there is room. The text gives no ground for assuming that anyone is too far out to be sent for.

study.originalLanguages:
Luke tells us in 14:1 that the guests were 'watching Him closely.' The Greek verb is paratereo, to observe with a purpose, to keep a careful eye on someone. Luke uses it for the scribes and Pharisees who watched to see whether Jesus would heal on the Sabbath in Luke 6:7 and for the spies who watched Him in 20:20. The grammar sets up a double observation: the experts are watching Jesus for a charge, and Jesus, who notices in 14:7 how the guests choose their seats, is watching them.

The seats of honor in 14:7 and 14:8 are the protoklisiai, literally the first reclining places. It is the same word Jesus uses when He charges the scribes with loving the best seats at banquets, Luke 20:46. The word ties the table in chapter 14 to the temple in chapter 20, and it shows that what He teaches here is not a matter of manners but of the same pride He later exposes.

When Jesus tells the host not to invite those who can pay him back, 14:12, He uses antapodoma, 'repayment,' and in 14:14 the verb antapodidomi, 'to be repaid.' Both belong to the language of the ledger. The same verb appears in Paul's question in Romans 11:35, which asks who has first given to God so that God must repay. The promise of 14:14 therefore takes the world's reciprocity and moves the payment to the resurrection of the righteous, where God is the one who settles accounts.

In the parable, the invited guests 'make excuses.' The verb is paraiteomai, to ask to be excused or to decline, and in 14:18 and 14:19 it appears in the polite formula 'have me excused.' The word has an official ring to it, the language of a request granted or refused. The guests treat the master's feast as a favor they can decline with a courtesy. The BSB's 'Please excuse me' keeps the tone, and the wry point is that all three are very polite and all three are refusing.

The call to count the cost uses a verb that is easy to miss, 14:28. 'Count' is psephizo, from the word for a pebble used in reckoning, and it appears in Revelation 13:18 where the reader is told to calculate the number of the beast. The disciple is asked to do careful arithmetic, as the builder and the king do.

When Jesus says in 14:33 that anyone who 'does not give up everything he has' cannot be His disciple, the verb is apotassomai, which in its ordinary use means to say goodbye or take leave. Luke uses it in 9:61 of the man who wants to say farewell to those at home. The word therefore does not describe mere abandonment but a formal taking of leave: the disciple bids farewell to every possession as a claim on the heart. The things themselves, the word that is rendered 'what he has,' are the hyparchonta, the possessions already named in Luke 12:15 and 12:33.

Finally, salt that 'loses its savor' in 14:34 is literally salt that has become foolish, from the verb moraino. Matthew 5:13 uses the same verb. The picture is of something that has stopped doing the one thing it is for, and the hearers are left to decide what a disciple is for.

typology.type: The feast on the mountain for all peoples, Isaiah 25:6-8
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah saw the LORD making a banquet of rich food for all peoples, swallowing up death and wiping away tears. Luke 14:15-24 shows that feast arriving in the person of Jesus, who eats with outsiders and sends servants to summon them. The correspondence deepens at the Last Supper, where Jesus promises His disciples that they will eat and drink at His table in His kingdom, Luke 22:30, and it is completed at the wedding supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9. The parable also falls short of the end it points to: the host here is a figure in a story, while the table in Revelation belongs to the risen Lord.

typology.type: The lowest place and the exalted servant
typology.fulfillment: The law of the table that the humble will be exalted is not only advice to guests. It is lived out by Jesus, who takes the place of a servant among His disciples, Luke 22:27, and who, in the hymn of Philippians 2:6-9, empties Himself, takes the form of a servant, humbles Himself to death on a cross, and is then highly exalted. The type is the guest who chooses the last seat; the fulfillment is the One who had every right to the first seat and chose the last. Where the guest humbles himself for a promotion that might follow, Christ's humbling was without calculation, and His exaltation is given to Him by the Father.

typology.type: The poor, crippled, lame and blind brought in
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 35:5-6 foretold the day when the eyes of the blind would be opened and the lame would leap, and Jesus told John's messengers that this was now happening, Luke 7:22. The parable gathers exactly these people into the house, and the dropsy healing at the opening of the chapter has already shown the host's table what Jesus' hospitality looks like. The fulfillment grows in Acts, where a man lame from birth is healed at the temple gate, Acts 3:1-10, and the church becomes a table that includes those once kept at the margins. The picture is not yet complete: the full restoration of bodies awaits the resurrection, which Jesus names in 14:14.

The call to carry one's cross and follow, Luke 14:27, finds its first literal picture when soldiers seize Simon of Cyrene and make him carry the cross behind Jesus, Luke 23:26. Simon was compelled, and the disciple goes willingly, but both walk where the Master walks. The pattern deepens in Hebrews 12:2, where Jesus endured the cross, scorning its shame, and in 13:13, where believers go to Him outside the camp. The type is limited in one respect: the disciple carries a cross behind Christ, but only Christ's own cross bears away sin.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ first as the Lord of the Sabbath who acts without hesitation. Where the experts in the law are silent, He takes hold of the sick man and heals him, Luke 14:4, and His question about the ox in the pit is answered by no one. The Sabbath, which Luke 13:10-17 has already shown to be a day for loosing the bound, becomes in 14:1-6 a day for restoring the swollen and the shamed. The first Sabbath meal in the chapter is thus not a pause in His ministry but its very pattern.

He is the host the chapter has been looking for. The feast the guest dreamed about in 14:15 is the feast Jesus is already hosting with tax collectors and sinners, and the servant who calls 'Come, for everything is now ready' speaks in a voice the first hearers would soon identify with His own. At the Last Supper He puts the same invitation into the form of bread and cup and promises that His disciples will eat and drink at His table in His kingdom, Luke 22:29-30. The invitation costs the guest nothing because it will cost the host everything, and the chapter hints at that cost when the master of the house is angry, 14:21, and when Jesus turns to describe a cross.

He is also the pattern of the humble. The law of 14:11 describes the path He walks: the One in the form of God took the form of a servant and was lifted up, Philippians 2:6-9. Luke gives the same note in 22:27, with His own description of Himself as the one who serves among them. When Jesus tells the guests to take the lowest place, He is not asking them to do something He will not do.

He is the one worth losing everything for. The claim of 14:26 is breathtaking for any teacher, and it would be blasphemy if He were less than the Lord. A rabbi might ask for the pupil's loyalty; Jesus asks for a loyalty that outranks father, mother, spouse, children and life. And He does not ask the crowd to carry what He will not carry. The cross He speaks of in 14:27 He will carry Himself, Luke 23:26-33, and the words of 14:28-32 about finishing what one begins are fulfilled when He sets His face toward Jerusalem, Luke 9:51, and does not turn back.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The tower, the king and the salt are not allegories of Christ; they are short illustrations of the need to reckon with a cost. And the master's anger in the parable is not a portrait of the Father cursing the poor, but of the host who will not be mocked. The chapter shows Christ not by decoding each detail but by who is speaking: the Man who heals on the Sabbath, hosts the outcast, humbles Himself, and asks for everything because He is about to give everything.
study.god:
The God of Luke 14 is first of all a God who gives a feast, and gives it on His own initiative. The master 'prepared a great banquet,' 14:16, and the invitation is sent with the words that everything is ready, 14:17. Nothing is left for the guests to supply. This is a God whose welcome precedes any worthiness, and the chapter's lists of the poor, the crippled, the lame and the blind show whom His hospitality is aimed at. The details of the parable show that His giving is not casual. The servant is sent twice, then again, and the master insists that the house be full.

He is a God who answers pride and humility differently. The saying of 14:11 is not a piece of social strategy but a statement about how God treats people. Those who grasp are brought low and those who lower themselves are lifted. The same God who opposes the proud gives grace to the humble, as James 4:6 says, quoting Proverbs 3:34. The picture of a host who moves a guest up or down shows God as the one who determines true honor, so that the scramble for it among people is already beside the point.

He is a God who keeps accounts and pays them. The promise of 14:14 that those who cannot repay will not go unrewarded means that nothing done for the poor is lost. God is the true debtor to every kindness done in secret. Yet it is a reward of grace, not wages, since the host who invites the poor does not earn anything that was not already promised.

He is a God who is jealous for His own invitation. The anger of the master in 14:21 and the verdict of 14:24 show that God does not take refusal lightly. The excuses were polite; the offense was real. The same God who makes the feast free is not indifferent to those who treat it as an inconvenience. Here the tension is held openly: grace is free and the refusal is serious.

Finally, He is a God whose claim is total. The language of 14:26 and 14:33 is possible only if the One who speaks is worthy of it. Worship, in this chapter, is not a mood but a verdict about what comes first. For a believer, the right response is the one the servant brings back in 14:22: 'what you ordered has been done, and there is still room,' meaning the church should go on inviting until the house is full, and should go on counting the cost with eyes open and the heart glad.

crossReferences.note: Wisdom had already taught not to put oneself forward in the king's presence, since it is better to be told to come up than to be humbled before a noble. The BSB footnote at Luke 14:10 points here. Jesus takes a piece of courtly advice and makes it a principle of the kingdom.

A man with a new house, a vineyard, or a betrothed wife could be excused from battle. The three excuses of Luke 14:18-20 sound like these exemptions, but where the law allowed them for war, the parable shows them used to avoid a feast, which exposes how small the reasons are against the greatness of the invitation.

The LORD prepares a banquet for all peoples and swallows up death. This is the hope behind the guest's cry in Luke 14:15, and the parable answers that the feast is ready and the invitation is open now, to those who will come.

Come, you who are thirsty, and you who have no money, buy and eat. The prophet's picture of free provision for the poor matches the master's gathering of the penniless in Luke 14:21 and explains why those with no claim are the ones who accept.

Jesus tells John's messengers that the blind see, the lame walk, and the poor have good news preached to them. The guests brought into the house in Luke 14:21 are the same people, which shows that the parable is not a new subject but a picture of what Jesus' ministry is already doing.

Whoever would come after Jesus must deny himself, take up his cross daily and follow. Luke 14:27 puts it again to a crowd, and the repetition across the travel narrative shows that the cost is not a one-time test but the shape of the whole road.

Three would-be followers meet their own excuses, the burying of a father, a farewell to family, a look backward. They are the personal versions of the three excuses in Luke 14:18-20 and the family claims of 14:26, and they show how readily good things become reasons not to follow.

Christ Jesus, being in the form of God, took the form of a servant and became obedient to death on a cross, and therefore God exalted Him. It is the law of Luke 14:11 played out in a single life, and it gives disciples both the pattern and the promise.

A related parable of a king's wedding feast, in which invited guests refuse and the hall is filled with others. The details differ, including the setting and the way the story ends, which shows Jesus using the image on more than one occasion for the same truth about refusing the invitation.

An angel says that those invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb are blessed. It answers the guest's cry in Luke 14:15 and shows that the banquet Jesus describes is the end toward which the Bible moves, with the invitation still open on the way.

Jesus suffered outside the gate, and believers are asked to go to Him outside the camp, bearing His reproach. It gives the cost of Luke 14:27 and 14:33 a concrete shape: to follow Him is to leave the safety of the settled place.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a table. In Genesis 1 and 2 God gives the man and the woman every tree for food, and the story of the fall begins when the gift is doubted and the one thing withheld is taken, Genesis 3:6. Everything after is a story of how God sets the table again for people who have walked away. Israel eats before the LORD at Sinai, Exodus 24:11, and in the land, feasts mark the year. The prophets look beyond, to the day when the LORD will spread a feast for all peoples and swallow up death, Isaiah 25:6-8.

Luke 14 is the moment when the host stands in the room. Jesus dines with those who watch Him and tells them that the feast is ready and that the guests list will not be the one they expect. The invited decline with polite excuses, and the ones who fill the house are those who had no place: the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame, then those from the highways and hedges beyond the city. The pattern runs through Luke and into Acts, where the good news goes out from Jerusalem to Samaria and to the ends of the earth, Acts 1:8, and the table opens to the nations.

The same chapter keeps the story honest about cost. The journey to Jerusalem is not a procession to a banquet but a march toward a cross, and anyone who follows must know it. The salt that has lost its savor reminds the reader that discipleship is not an ornament but a usefulness, and that a people who are fed freely are meant to be good for something in the world.

The story then moves toward its end in two ways. First, the Lord's Supper takes up the invitation: at a table in an upper room Jesus gives bread and cup and promises a place at His table in His kingdom, Luke 22:14-20 and 22:29-30. Second, the cross itself is the price of the feast. He who humbled Himself and was exalted opens the way for everyone who will come.

In the new creation the parable's last line is fulfilled in a way no one expected. The house is full, and those invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb are called blessed, Revelation 19:9. The tables of the proud are gone, the lists of repayment are abolished, and the table of the Lamb is surrounded by people from every nation, Revelation 7:9, who could never have repaid the host and who sit down because they were asked.

quiz.q: What lesson does Jesus draw from how the guests chose their seats?

options.text: Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted.
options.note: Luke 14:11 states the kingdom's reversal directly.

options.text: It is wiser to take a low seat so the host can move you up.
options.note: True to the parable's picture, but it is the servant illustration, not the deeper principle of God humbling and exalting.

options.text: Good manners will win you the respect of others.
options.note: The point is God's exalting of the humble, not social technique to gain esteem.

options.text: Those who seize the best seats deserve them.
options.note: The opposite: the self-exalting will be humbled.

quiz.q: Why does Jesus tell the host to invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind?

options.text: Because they cannot repay, so the host will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.
options.note: Luke 14:13-14 grounds the invitation in reward from God, not reciprocity.

options.text: Because generosity to the needy is blessed by God.
options.note: True, but it omits the specific ground: they cannot repay, and God repays at the resurrection.

options.text: Because the poor make more grateful guests.
options.note: The reason given is the inability to repay and God's future reward, not the guests' gratitude.

options.text: Because inviting rich neighbors is forbidden.
options.note: Jesus warns against inviting only those who can repay, not against rich people as such.

quiz.q: What happens in the parable of the great banquet?

options.text: The invited guests make excuses, so the master fills his house with the poor and the outsiders.
options.note: Luke 14:18-23 shows the refusal of the first-invited and the gathering of the unlikely.

options.text: The master gathers the poor from the streets into his house.
options.note: True, but it leaves out the crucial refusal of the originally invited guests.

options.text: The guests were too busy but promised to come later.
options.note: They did not defer; they refused, and none of them will taste the banquet.

options.text: The banquet was canceled because no one came.
options.note: The house is filled to overflowing; the feast goes ahead with new guests.

quiz.q: What does Jesus say it costs to be His disciple?

options.text: To put Him above family and self, carry one's cross, and give up everything.
options.note: Luke 14:26-33 names supreme allegiance, cross-bearing, and total surrender.

options.text: To love Christ more than father, mother, and one's own life.
options.note: True and central, but it omits cross-bearing and the surrender of everything.

options.text: To perform acts of self-denial from time to time.
options.note: Jesus asks not occasional gestures but a daily cross and the giving up of all.

options.text: Nothing; following Jesus makes no real demands.
options.note: The whole passage is about counting the cost, which is total.

quiz.q: What is the warning of the savorless salt?

options.text: A disciple who loses what makes him distinct becomes useless and is thrown out.
options.note: Luke 14:34-35 warns against a discipleship that has lost its savor.

options.text: Salt is a good and useful thing.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but the warning is about salt that has lost its savor.

options.text: Disciples should season their speech with grace.
options.note: A worthy idea elsewhere, but here the image warns of uselessness, not of gracious speech.

options.text: Salt can never lose its usefulness.
options.note: The point is precisely that savorless salt is fit for nothing and discarded.

questions: Jesus watched people reach for the best seats. Where are you quietly maneuvering for status, and what would it look like to take the lowest place and trust God to lift you?
The host is told to invite those who cannot repay. Who might God be asking you to welcome with no return in view, looking instead to the resurrection?
In the parable the guests were not wicked, just busy with a field, oxen, and a marriage. Which good and ordinary things are you letting crowd out God's invitation?
Jesus tells the eager crowds to count the cost. Have you ever honestly reckoned what following Him may cost you, and does He hold first place over every other love?
Grace fills the banquet for free, yet it lays a cross on every guest. Where is Christ calling you to a daily death this week, and what makes that hard to carry?

translationNotes.note: A footnote records that some manuscripts read 'donkey' rather than 'son'; either way the point is that people rescue what is theirs on the Sabbath, so surely a suffering person may be healed.

The Greek verb rendered 'hate' is a Semitic idiom for loving less or subordinating. Matthew's parallel, 'loves father or mother more than Me', confirms the sense: Christ demands supreme allegiance, not literal hatred, and elsewhere He upholds honoring parents.
'He who has ears to hear, let him hear' is Jesus' recurring call to attend and obey, sharpening the warning that a savorless discipleship is discarded.
